deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page and this page). Hilbert is proving a theorem he calls 'obiger Satz': a finite group G of n-ary linear substitutions can be written so that all coefficients are rational in roots of unity. In this passage he treats the case where G contains an element A with n distinct characteristic roots α_1,…,α_n. All of these are roots of unity, since A has finite order. Choose variables so that A = diag(α_1,…,α_n). Fraktur letters 𝔄=(a_ij) and 𝔅=(b_ij) denote arbitrary elements of G.

Step 0 (previous page; the basic fact). Every group element has finite order, so its characteristic roots are roots of unity. Its trace, and hence each power sum of its roots, lies in a cyclotomic field. In particular, the 'first coefficient of the characteristic equation' of A^k𝔄 is cyclotomic for every k.

Step 1 (previous page). tr(A^k 𝔄) = Σ_i α_i^k a_ii for k = 0,…,n-1. The coefficient matrix (α_i^k) is a Vandermonde matrix, and it is invertible because the α_i are distinct. Hence every diagonal entry a_ii of every group element lies in Q(roots of unity).

Step 2 (previous page). Apply Step 1 to the group elements 𝔄A^k𝔄. Their (1,1) entry is Σ_j α_j^k a_1j a_j1, which is the '𝔄², α𝔄², α²𝔄², …' computation. By Vandermonde again, each product a_1j a_j1 is cyclotomic.

Hilbert then concludes that a_21,…,a_n1 themselves are cyclotomic. This silently uses a normalisation that is mine to supply: the only freedom left is conjugation by diagonal matrices D, which commute with A and send a_ij to (d_i/d_j) a_ij. One may scale so that a_1j = 1 (or another cyclotomic value) whenever a_1j ≠ 0.

Step 3 (top of this page). Compute the (1,1) entries of 𝔄𝔅, A𝔄𝔅, A²𝔄𝔅, …. In general (𝔄A^k𝔅)_11 = Σ_j a_1j α_j^k b_j1. After the normalisation a_1j = 1 this becomes Σ_j α_j^k b_j·. These are the displayed expressions:
- b_12 + b_22 + b_32 + …
- α_1 b_12 + α_2 b_22 + …
- α_1² b_12 + α_2² b_22 + …

All of them are cyclotomic. By Vandermonde, the individual b's are cyclotomic. Hilbert's index order for b here appears to be (column, row), or else he is slightly loose about it. He reads off 'in particular the first entry of the 2nd horizontal row of every group element is cyclotomic'.

Step 4. Apply this fact to the elements 𝔄𝔅, A𝔄𝔅, A²𝔄𝔅, …. Their entry in that position is a Vandermonde-type combination of the entries of the 2nd vertical row (column) of 𝔅. Hence the whole 2nd column of 𝔅 is cyclotomic, 'und so fort' for the remaining rows and columns.

Conclusion. The theorem is proved when G contains a substitution whose characteristic equation has only distinct roots.

Clean modern version (my completion). For any X,Y,Z in G and any k,l:
(X A^k Y A^l Z)_11 = Σ_{i,j} x_1i α_i^k y_ij α_j^l z_j1.
The two-variable Vandermonde argument then gives that every product x_1i y_ij z_j1 is cyclotomic. If G is irreducible, one can choose X, Z and a diagonal rescaling with x_1i, z_j1 nonzero and cyclotomic, and so all y_ij are cyclotomic.

The last line starts a new topic: a plan to prove Picard's theorems on entire transcendental functions directly, without modular functions. It continues on the next page.
errors: The passage from 'a_1j a_j1 cyclotomic' to 'a_j1 cyclotomic' requires a diagonal renormalisation (allowed since diagonal matrices commute with A) and the non-vanishing of the relevant a_1j. Neither is stated.

Irreducibility, or a reduction to the irreducible case, is tacitly needed. Otherwise some off-diagonal entries can vanish identically and the normalisation is not available. A reducible group is fine after splitting it, but this is not mentioned.

The index bookkeeping on this page is loose. The displayed sums run over b_12, b_22, b_32 (first index varying), yet the conclusion is phrased as 'first element of the 2nd horizontal row', which would be b_21 in row-column convention. Either Hilbert writes b_(column,row) or the step is sketched carelessly. The mathematics can be repaired as in the reconstruction.
'u.s.fort' hides the induction over the remaining rows and columns. It is routine but not written out.

results.what: If a finite linear group contains an element with pairwise distinct eigenvalues, then in the basis diagonalising it (suitably rescaled) all matrix coefficients of all group elements lie in a cyclotomic field. Proof via traces and Vandermonde inversion.
results.modern_name: Realisability of finite group representations over cyclotomic fields (special case of Schur's conjecture / Brauer's splitting field theorem); the 'regular element' case
results.usually_credited_to: H. Maschke, Math. Ann. 50 (1898), 'Über den arithmetischen Charakter der Coefficienten der Substitutionen endlicher linearer Substitutionsgruppen' (my recollection is that he proved essentially this case). General case conjectured by Schur (1906), proved by R. Brauer (1945/47).

results.what: Recovering the diagonal entries (and products a_1j a_j1) from cyclotomic traces tr(A^k X) by inverting a Vandermonde system in the distinct eigenvalues α_i.
Plan (only begun here) to prove Picard's theorem for entire functions without modular functions, via level curves |f|=m.
results.modern_name: Elementary proof of Picard's little theorem
results.usually_credited_to: E. Borel (1896), first elementary proof; Picard (1879) via the modular function

deep.surprise_reason: To my recollection this exact special case (a group containing an element with distinct characteristic roots) was published by Maschke in 1898. That paper was part of the program that led to Maschke's complete-reducibility theorem. Hilbert's note looks like a reworking or anticipation of that argument, depending on the notebook's date. It is a nice unpublished trace of Hilbert's interest, not a new result. If the page predates 1898 it would be mildly more notable.

checkable.asserts: The Vandermonde determinant factorises as a product of differences. It is nonzero iff the α_i are distinct, so the trace systems are uniquely solvable.

checkable.sympy: X=Matrix(3,3,symbols('x11:14 x21:24 x31:34')); a=symbols('a1:4'); A=diag(*a); k=2; expand((A**k*X).trace() - sum(a[i]**k*X[i,i] for i in range(3)))
checkable.asserts: tr(A^k X) = Σ α_i^k x_ii (Step 1). Should give 0.

checkable.sympy: X=Matrix(3,3,symbols('x11:14 x21:24 x31:34')); Y=Matrix(3,3,symbols('y11:14 y21:24 y31:34')); a=symbols('a1:4'); A=diag(*a); k=3; expand((X*A**k*Y)[0,0] - sum(X[0,j]*a[j]**k*Y[j,0] for j in range(3)))
checkable.asserts: (X A^k Y)_11 = Σ_j x_1j α_j^k y_j1 (Steps 2–3). Should give 0.

checkable.sympy: X=Matrix(3,3,symbols('x11:14 x21:24 x31:34')); d=symbols('d1:4'); D=diag(*d); simplify((D*X*D.inv())[0,1] - d[0]/d[1]*X[0,1])
checkable.asserts: Conjugation by a diagonal matrix (which commutes with A) rescales a_ij by d_i/d_j. This is the freedom used for the implicit normalisation. Should give 0.

transcription_corrections: 'A^0 A B, A A B, A^2 A B' should read '𝔄𝔅, A𝔄𝔅, A²𝔄𝔅' (fraktur 𝔄, 𝔅 for general group elements; Latin A for the diagonal element). Likewise 'Substitution B' is fraktur 𝔅.

'Hiermit ist obige Satz für den Fall {+bewiesen+}': 'bewiesen' is a superscript insertion placed after 'Fall'. The parenthesis opens before 'dass', so the clause reads 'für den Fall (dass eine Substitution A in der Gruppe existirt, deren charakteristische Gl. lauter verschiedene Wurzeln besitzt) bewiesen'.
Last line: 'Suche die Picard'schen Sätze über ganze transcenden-' is correct; it continues on the next page with '…te Funktionen direct… zu beweisen'.
